title: How to Test Text-to-Speech Medical Interpretation Voices
summary: Test text-to-speech medical interpretation voice quality across pacing, tone, pronunciation, devices, and patient understanding before buying.
body_markdown:
###


Read complete dosing instructions aloud on the actual device your staff will use, then ask a listener to transcribe what they heard. Compare "0.5 mg" and "5 mg" spoken output directly, since these doses differ tenfold and a pronunciation gap alone can change clinical meaning.


###


A focused pilot on one language and one medication-counseling script can expose consequential failures in pacing, pronunciation, and interrupted playback, but it cannot support approval across untested languages or channels. Extend testing to cover each device type, telehealth, and phone workflows before expanding deployment.


###


Teach-back asks patients to describe the plan in their own words, confirming that spoken interpretation produced real understanding and not merely audible output. When a patient cannot explain their next steps correctly, pause the exchange, identify the unclear content, ask the original speaker to clarify, and verify the corrected interpretation before continuing.


###


No. Select voices based on tested comprehension and patient-stated preference, not on age, ethnicity, or other demographic characteristics. Ask patients whether the available voice feels comfortable and understandable, then document preferences through your standard workflow.


###


Compare the translated text against the source first, then compare the audio against that translated text. This two-step check routes wording errors to your translation review process and pronunciation or playback errors to your voice-output review, keeping incident reports actionable.
